newsitem.title: UK: Britain, pushing ethics, hosts Nigeria talks.
newsitem.headline: Britain, pushing ethics, hosts Nigeria talks.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government, which has pledged to put ethics at the heart of foreign policy, hosts talks on Thursday over Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth.
Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in 1995 after its military-led administration executed Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight minority rights activists despite widespread clemency appeals.

The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) will spend the day listening to Nigerian opposition groups and human rights organisations to help it decide whether to recommend tougher action by Commonwealth states against Nigeria.

This week's session will gather information for a crunch meeting in September when the eight-nation ministerial group will finalise its recommendation to a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), to be held a month later.
Diplomats and campaigners said the meeting will set the stage for a key test of the Labour government's stated commitment to ethics in foreign policy.

"This is going to be the first opportunity for the new British government to put teeth into its several pre- and post-election declarations," said Professor Bolaji Akinyemi of the opposition National Democratic Coalition of Nigeria.
"We are mildly optimistic that at least Britain is going to be on the side of CMAG (nations) who have been urging more effective measures against Nigeria," Akinyemi told Reuters.
The 53-member Commonwealth groups largely members of the former British Empire.
Foreign Secretary Robin Cook sharply criticised Nigeria two weeks ago, accusing its military government of corruption and saying it should remain suspended from the Commonwealth.
"Nigeria is a very interesting example of the way in which economic progress and human rights are complementary. Nigeria should not be a poor country

"It has huge natural resources and every potential to be one of the two most wealthy countries in Africa. What holds it back is a corrupt regime and very poor standards of democratic government," Cook told reporters.
A statement from the Nigerian foreign ministry said Cook's remarks were "hostile" and "not only malicious but prejudicial to our good standing in the international community".
Nigeria's military ruler, General Sani Abacha, has promised to hand power to an elected president next year.

But delays in the schedule of elections, dismissed in any case by opponents as a ruse to ensure continued military control of the West African oil giant, have added to widespread doubts about the military's pledge.
Cook said after the May 1 election which put Labour in power that the world should be prepared to apply sanctions against Nigeria until it returned to the democratic fold.
Britain's previous Conservative administration never fully backed sanctions, saying they could hurt ordinary Nigerians.
Cook's call for a tougher response has been backed by states like Canada. But splits in the ministerial group have so far prevented tougher Commonwealth action.
Akinyemi's National Democratic Coalition is one of the opposition groups due to address the meeting. Human rights bodies like Amnesty International will also be there.
Akinyemi said he was optimistic the change of government in Britain would increase the probability that Nigeria's suspension would be continued and that sanctions would be tightened.

"There's going to be a change in chemistry...Canada, Jamaica, New Zealand have been the minority (on the CMAG) holding the flame of democracy. Britain played a very lukewarm role...All that is going to change," he said.
